questions.prompt: In Android's testing guidance, which description matches a **fake**?

choices.text: A test double you program to return canned answers, with no expectations about how it is called
A test double with a working but test-only implementation, such as an in-memory database
A test double that fails the test if its calls don't match the expected interactions
A wrapper around a real object that records calls made to it

sources.claim: A fake has a working implementation unsuitable for production (e.g. an in-memory database); a mock has expectations about interactions; a stub has none; a spy wraps a real object. Fakes are lightweight and preferred.
sources.title: Use test doubles in Android

questions.explanation: A fake is a working implementation that is fine for tests but not for production, such as an in-memory repository. Canned answers with no interaction checks describe a stub; failing on unexpected interactions is a mock; wrapping a real object is a spy. The guide prefers fakes because they need no mocking framework and stay lightweight.

questions.prompt: A ViewModel builds its own `Retrofit` client and calls `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` directly. Local tests are slow and flaky. Which change most improves testability?

choices.text: Move the logic into the Activity so it can be exercised end to end with an Espresso instrumented test running on a real device
Wrap every test in `Thread.sleep(500)` so the background IO work has time to finish before the assertions run
Mock the `Dispatchers.IO` object itself with `mockkStatic` so it executes on the calling test thread instead of a background one
Inject the repository through an interface and inject the dispatcher, so tests pass a fake and a `TestDispatcher`

sources.claim: Avoid adding logic to activities and fragments, avoid framework dependencies in business logic, and make dependencies easy to replace, for example with interfaces instead of concrete implementations.
sources.title: Fundamentals of testing Android apps

sources.claim: Inject dispatchers so tests can replace them with TestDispatchers that share runTest's scheduler.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin coroutines on Android

questions.explanation: The guide recommends replaceable dependencies (interfaces rather than concrete classes, injected) and injecting dispatchers so tests can use a `TestDispatcher` sharing the test scheduler. That makes tests fast and deterministic. Moving logic into Activities goes against the guidance, sleeps cause flakiness, and static-mocking dispatchers is fragile.

questions.prompt: A test creates `val repo = mockk<UserRepository>()` and the code under test calls `repo.lastSync()`, which the test never stubbed. What happens?

choices.text: The call throws, because MockK mocks are strict by default and need behaviour stubbed for every call that is made on them
The call quietly returns `null`, because MockK mocks return sensible default values for any function nobody bothered to stub
The call transparently falls through and runs the real `UserRepository.lastSync()` implementation on the actual backing class
The call is simply recorded, and the test still passes as long as nobody later calls `confirmVerified(repo)` on that mock

sources.claim: By default mocks are strict, so you need to provide some behaviour; a relaxed mock (relaxed = true) returns simple values for all functions; spyk mixes mocks and real objects.
sources.title: MockK

questions.explanation: MockK mocks are strict by default: calling an unstubbed function fails. Returning simple defaults requires `mockk(relaxed = true)`, and calling real code requires `spyk`. Strictness catches unexpected interactions, but it also ties tests to implementation details.

questions.prompt: You need to stub a `suspend fun fetchUser(id: String): User` on a MockK mock and later check that it was called once. Which pair is correct?

choices.text: `every { api.fetchUser("1") } returns user` and `verify(exactly = 1) { api.fetchUser("1") }`
`whenever(api.fetchUser("1")).thenReturn(user)` and `verify(api).fetchUser("1")`
`coEvery { api.fetchUser("1") } returns user` and `coVerify(exactly = 1) { api.fetchUser("1") }`
`spyk(api)` and `confirmVerified(api)`

sources.claim: MockK provides coEvery and coVerify for suspend functions, verify(exactly = n) for call counts, and confirmVerified to ensure all recorded calls were verified.
sources.title: MockK

questions.explanation: Suspend functions are stubbed and verified with the coroutine variants `coEvery` and `coVerify`; `exactly = 1` sets the call count. Plain `every`/`verify` are for regular functions, `whenever`/`thenReturn` is Mockito-Kotlin syntax, and `confirmVerified` only checks that every recorded call was verified.

questions.prompt: According to Android's testing strategy guidance, how should tests be distributed, and why?

choices.text: Mostly end-to-end tests running on real devices, because only a full device test reflects what a real user actually experiences
Roughly equal numbers of unit, integration and end-to-end tests, so the suite gives balanced coverage across every layer of the app
Only instrumented tests, because local JVM tests are unable to exercise any genuine Android framework API at all
Many small tests and few big ones, since small tests are fast and cheap while big tests are slower and costlier

sources.claim: Most apps should have many small tests and relatively few big tests, forming a pyramid; a bug caught by a unit test is typically fixed in minutes, while an end-to-end test could take days to discover it.
sources.title: Testing strategies

questions.explanation: The guidance describes a pyramid: many small tests at the base and relatively few big tests at the top. A bug caught by a unit test is usually fixed in minutes, while an end-to-end test might take days to find the same bug. Big tests have higher fidelity but are slower and more prone to flakiness, so they're used for critical journeys.

questions.prompt: A repository test uses MockK to stub five DAO and API calls and then verifies the exact order of calls. Every refactor breaks it, even when behaviour is unchanged. Explain why, and rewrite the approach using fakes. When is a mock still the right choice?

sources.claim: Mocks have expectations about interactions and fail tests if they don't match; fakes have working implementations, don't require a mocking framework, are lightweight and are preferred.
sources.title: Use test doubles in Android

sources.claim: MockK mocks are strict by default and support verify(exactly = n) and ordering checks, which enforce specific interactions.
sources.title: MockK

questions.explanation: The senior answer is not 'mocks bad', it is choosing the double by what is being asserted. Android's guidance prefers fakes, and a good candidate explains the maintenance cost of over-specified mocks.

model_answer.summary: Interaction-heavy mocks tie tests to implementation details (which calls, in what order), so refactors break them. Fakes, such as an in-memory DAO and a fake API, let the test assert on observable outcomes. Keep mocks for verifying interactions that are the behaviour itself, such as 'analytics event sent once'.
key_points: Mocks with strict expectations encode how the code works, not what it does, so behaviour-preserving refactors fail tests
A fake is a working lightweight implementation (in-memory DAO, fake network source) that needs no mocking framework
With fakes, arrange state, run the operation, and assert on results or emitted data (for example cache-then-network), not on the call sequence
Fakes can be shared across tests and modules, for example in a test module, so they get maintained once
Mocks still fit when the interaction is the contract: a side effect with no observable state, such as sending an event exactly once

questions.prompt: You inherit a feature where a Fragment calls Retrofit, writes to Room, and uses `GlobalScope.launch(Dispatchers.IO)`. Describe the refactor that makes it testable, and which tests you would write at each layer afterwards.

sources.claim: Split the app into layers, avoid logic in activities and fragments, avoid framework dependencies in business logic, and use dependency injection with interfaces; untestable architecture gives bigger, slower, more flaky tests.
sources.title: Fundamentals of testing Android apps

sources.claim: Replace real dispatchers with injected TestDispatchers for deterministic tests.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin coroutines on Android

questions.explanation: Senior candidates tie each refactor step to what it enables in tests and follow the guidance: no logic in framework classes, replaceable dependencies, controllable dispatchers.

model_answer.summary: Move logic out of the Fragment into a ViewModel and a repository behind interfaces, inject dependencies (DI) and dispatchers, and use structured scopes. Then write local unit tests for the ViewModel with fakes and `runTest`, repository tests with fakes or an in-memory Room, and a few UI tests.
key_points: Split into layers: UI (Fragment/Compose) only renders state; a ViewModel holds presentation logic; a repository owns data access
Put interfaces at the boundaries (API, DAO, repository) and inject them, so tests can substitute fakes
Inject the `CoroutineDispatcher` and replace `GlobalScope` with `viewModelScope` or an injected scope, so tests control scheduling with a `TestDispatcher`
Remove Android framework types (Context) from business logic so it runs in fast local JVM tests
Then test: ViewModel state tests (local), repository tests with fakes or an in-memory database, and a small number of UI tests for critical flows

questions.prompt: You have a one-day take-home (fetch, list, detail, offline). How do you decide what to test with the time you have, and what do you write in the README about testing?

sources.claim: Repository tests should cover online/offline and with/without cached data; ViewModel tests can be noted where time is short; add a README that pastes the rubric and marks each item done.
sources.title: Android job interview take-home test cheat sheet

sources.claim: Start with small tests early; many small tests and relatively few big tests.
sources.title: Testing strategies

questions.explanation: Reviewers look for judgment: tests at the right layer with the right doubles, and an honest account of gaps. Covering everything shallowly scores lower than covering the risky data logic well.

model_answer.summary: Put tests where the logic and risk are: repository tests for online, offline and cached scenarios, and ViewModel state tests, with fakes at the boundaries. Add one UI test for the main flow if time allows. Use the README to map the rubric, explain trade-offs, and list the tests you would add next.
key_points: Prioritize repository tests: online/offline and with/without cached data, since the offline logic is what reviewers check
ViewModel tests for loading, success and error states using fakes and a test dispatcher
A small number of UI tests (or one Compose test) for the main list-to-detail flow, following the pyramid
README: paste the rubric, mark each item done, and explain testing choices and what you would add with more time
Tests should be deterministic and fast, with no real network calls or sleeps

questions.prompt: A ViewModel's `uiState: StateFlow<UiState>` moves quickly through `Loading` to `Success`. A test that collects every emission and expects `[Loading, Success]` sometimes gets only `[Success]`. What is the recommended fix?

choices.text: Add an artificial `delay(100)` between the `Loading` and `Success` emissions inside the ViewModel so the test has time to observe both
Collect the flow with `.buffer(Channel.UNLIMITED)` applied downstream, so that every intermediate value is queued and none is dropped
Treat the `StateFlow` as a state holder: drive the fake step by step and assert on `uiState.value` at each point
Switch the ViewModel's exposed type to a `SharedFlow` configured with `replay = 0`, so every collector sees every emission in order

sources.claim: StateFlow is conflated, so collectors are not guaranteed to receive all intermediate values; we generally recommend treating StateFlow as a data holder and asserting on its value property.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin flows on Android

questions.explanation: `StateFlow` is conflated, so collectors aren't guaranteed to see intermediate values, only the latest. The guidance recommends asserting on `value` after each controlled step. Buffering downstream can't recover values the conflated flow never delivered, and changing production code or adding delays to suit a test is the wrong direction.

questions.prompt: The ViewModel exposes `repo.scores().map { ... }.stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), 0)`. The test emits from a fake repository and asserts on `viewModel.score.value`, but it always stays `0`. Why?

choices.text: With `WhileSubscribed`, upstream isn't collected until there's a subscriber; start one in `backgroundScope` with `UnconfinedTestDispatcher`
`stateIn` with `WhileSubscribed(5_000)` always needs an explicit `advanceTimeBy(5_000)` call before its very first value becomes available
The `.value` property is simply never updated at all for any `StateFlow` that was created through the `stateIn` operator
The fake repository's `scores()` function must itself return a `StateFlow` rather than a plain `Flow` for `stateIn` to work correctly

sources.claim: When testing a StateFlow created with stateIn and WhileSubscribed, there must be at least one collector; create an empty collector in backgroundScope with UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler).
sources.title: Testing Kotlin flows on Android

questions.explanation: `WhileSubscribed` starts sharing only while there's at least one subscriber, and reading `.value` doesn't subscribe. The documented pattern launches an empty collector in `backgroundScope` using `UnconfinedTestDispatcher(testScheduler)`. The 5-second value is the stop timeout, not a start delay.

questions.prompt: A test class creates `private val dispatcher = StandardTestDispatcher()` as a field and passes it to the repository, then the test body uses `runTest { ... advanceUntilIdle() ... }`. Work launched on the repository's dispatcher never runs. Why?

choices.text: `StandardTestDispatcher` runs every coroutine eagerly and immediately, so any later call to `advanceUntilIdle()` has nothing left to do
The field's dispatcher has its own separate scheduler; advancing `runTest`'s doesn't run it, so all dispatchers must share one
`advanceUntilIdle()` only drains work scheduled specifically on `Dispatchers.Main`, never on any other injected dispatcher
`runTest` automatically cancels any coroutine that was launched on a dispatcher injected from outside the test body itself

sources.claim: There must be only one TestCoroutineScheduler shared between all TestDispatchers in a test; creating a dispatcher with StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler) shares runTest's scheduler; TestDispatchers created after Dispatchers.setMain use Main's scheduler.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin coroutines on Android

questions.explanation: Each `TestDispatcher` created without a scheduler gets a new one unless `Dispatchers.Main` was set to a test dispatcher first. Coroutines on a different scheduler aren't advanced by `runTest`'s `advanceUntilIdle()`. Fix it by creating the dispatcher inside the test with `StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)`, or set Main first (for example with a `MainDispatcherRule`). `StandardTestDispatcher` queues work; it is `Unconfined` that runs eagerly.

questions.prompt: You want fast, hermetic tests of your Room DAOs. Which approach matches the current Room testing guidance?

choices.text: Build with `Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder(...)`, close it in `@After`, and run on device or the JVM with `BundledSQLiteDriver`
Mock each DAO interface with MockK and assert that the expected query methods were called with the expected arguments
Use the real on-disk production database file for every test class, so results match production and tests can share seeded data
Run DAO tests as Robolectric local tests, which the current Room documentation names as its recommended approach for DAOs

sources.claim: Create an in-memory database with Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder for hermetic tests and close it in @After; BundledSQLiteDriver uses the same SQLite version across host and devices; Robolectric local tests are not recommended.
sources.title: Test and debug your database

questions.explanation: An in-memory database disappears when the process ends, which keeps tests hermetic, and it must be closed in `@After`. The guidance recommends device tests, or host JVM tests with `BundledSQLiteDriver` for a consistent SQLite version, and explicitly does not recommend Robolectric for this. Mocking the DAO tests nothing about your SQL, and a shared on-disk file leaks state between tests.

questions.prompt: In a Turbine `flow.test { ... }` block, you assert on the first item and the block ends while the flow has already emitted a second item. What happens?

choices.text: The test passes silently; Turbine drops any event nobody explicitly asserted on once the `test { }` block finishes
The test hangs and only fails once `runTest`'s own default 60-second coroutine timeout is finally reached
Turbine automatically calls `awaitComplete()` on the flow's behalf before the block exits, consuming whatever is left
The test fails with an 'Unconsumed events found' error; call `cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()` to opt out on purpose

sources.claim: test launches a coroutine that collects the flow, then cancels it and calls ensureAllEventsConsumed(); unconsumed events fail with 'Unconsumed events found'; cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents() skips that check; default timeout is 3 seconds of wall-clock time.
sources.title: Turbine

questions.explanation: At the end of `test`, Turbine cancels collection and calls `ensureAllEventsConsumed()`, so leftover items fail the test. That catches unexpected emissions. `cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()` opts out on purpose. Turbine's own wait timeout is 3 seconds of wall-clock time, not virtual time.

questions.prompt: Explain how you set up local unit tests for a ViewModel that launches work in `viewModelScope` and calls a repository that switches to an injected IO dispatcher. Compare `StandardTestDispatcher` and `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` and say when you use each.

sources.claim: runTest skips delays and has a 60-second default timeout; StandardTestDispatcher queues coroutines and needs advanceUntilIdle or runCurrent; UnconfinedTestDispatcher runs eagerly; use a MainDispatcherRule with setMain/resetMain; share a single scheduler.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin coroutines on Android

questions.explanation: The trap seniors avoid is multiple schedulers. A strong answer also explains that `StandardTestDispatcher` is what lets you observe `Loading` before `Success`.

model_answer.summary: Replace `Dispatchers.Main` with a test dispatcher through a `MainDispatcherRule`, inject a test dispatcher into the repository that shares the same scheduler, and write the test in `runTest`. `StandardTestDispatcher` queues coroutines and needs `advanceUntilIdle()` or `runCurrent()`, giving control over ordering; `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` runs eagerly, which is simpler but less like production.
key_points: `viewModelScope` uses `Dispatchers.Main`, which isn't available in local tests, so use `Dispatchers.setMain`/`resetMain`, usually in a `MainDispatcherRule`
Inject the repository's dispatcher and use a `TestDispatcher` that shares one `TestCoroutineScheduler` with `runTest`
`runTest` skips `delay` with virtual time and waits for coroutines on test dispatchers; its default timeout is 60 seconds
`StandardTestDispatcher` queues new coroutines until the test yields (`advanceUntilIdle`, `runCurrent`, `advanceTimeBy`), so intermediate states like Loading can be asserted
`UnconfinedTestDispatcher` starts coroutines eagerly; it's convenient for collectors in `backgroundScope` but hides ordering and concurrency issues

questions.prompt: Write out (in words or pseudo-code) a Turbine-based test plan for a repository flow `observeArticles()` that emits the cached list, then the refreshed network list, and reports an error if the network fails. What pitfalls do you watch for?

sources.claim: awaitItem, awaitComplete and awaitError assert emissions; unconsumed events fail the test; expectMostRecentItem returns the latest item; the default timeout is 3 seconds wall-clock.
sources.title: Turbine

sources.claim: Use fake repositories that emit flows; Turbine offers a convenient API for testing flows inside runTest.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin flows on Android

questions.explanation: Strong answers show why Turbine helps: it makes the order of emissions explicit and fails on unexpected extra events. They also know where it doesn't fit, such as conflated state.

model_answer.summary: Use a fake data source you control, run `observeArticles().test { }` inside `runTest`, and assert with `awaitItem()` for the cached then refreshed lists, `awaitError()` or an error state for failure, and `awaitComplete()` if the flow ends. Mind the unconsumed-events check, StateFlow conflation, and Turbine's wall-clock timeout.
key_points: Arrange a fake local and network source; start collecting with `flow.test { }` inside `runTest`
Success: `awaitItem()` equals the cached list, then trigger or emit the network result, and `awaitItem()` equals the refreshed list
Failure: the fake throws and you assert `awaitError()` (or an error item if errors are modelled as values)
Every event must be consumed or the block fails; use `cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents()` only on purpose for infinite flows
Turbine's 3-second timeout is wall-clock time; for conflated `StateFlow`s prefer asserting on `value` or `expectMostRecentItem()`

questions.prompt: Your offline-first repository reads from Room and refreshes from the network. Describe how you test the DAO queries and the repository's cache behaviour, including where each test runs and why.

sources.claim: Use an in-memory database for hermetic tests and close it in @After; Room KMP supports host JVM tests with BundledSQLiteDriver, which uses the same SQLite version everywhere; Robolectric is not recommended; see Testing Migrations for migrations.
sources.title: Test and debug your database

questions.explanation: A senior answer puts each test at the right fidelity: real SQL for DAOs and fakes at the network boundary. Mentioning the SQLite-version issue that `BundledSQLiteDriver` solves shows current knowledge.

model_answer.summary: Test DAOs against a real in-memory Room database (on device, or on the JVM with `BundledSQLiteDriver`), because that exercises your actual SQL. Test the repository's cache and refresh policy with that database or a fake DAO plus a fake network source, asserting on the emitted data in `runTest`.
key_points: DAO tests use `Room.inMemoryDatabaseBuilder` so data is discarded with the process and tests are hermetic; close the database in `@After`
Run them as instrumented tests or as host JVM tests with `BundledSQLiteDriver` so the SQLite version matches; Robolectric isn't recommended for Room
Don't mock DAOs to test queries, since that tests nothing about the SQL or the Flow invalidation
Repository tests: fake network source for success, failure and offline; assert the flow emits cached data first, then updated data after refresh
Test migrations separately with exported schemas

questions.prompt: A `Button` contains `Row { Icon(...); Text("Pay"); Text("$20") }`. The test `onNodeWithText("$20").assertIsDisplayed()` finds the button node, but `onNodeWithText("$20").assertTextEquals("$20")` fails. Why?

choices.text: By default finders search the merged tree, where the Button's children merge into one node with both strings; use `useUnmergedTree = true`
`onNodeWithText` only ever matches a node's `contentDescription` property, and never matches the literal text drawn by a `Text` composable in the tree
The `Icon` composable placed before the two `Text` nodes blocks semantics reporting for every one of its sibling composables
Text rendered inside a `Button` composable isn't merged into the semantics tree that Compose test finders search at all

sources.claim: By default semantics information is merged; a Button with Text children merges into a single node; set useUnmergedTree = true to access unmerged children.
sources.title: Testing APIs (Compose)

sources.claim: Tests find elements through the semantics tree with finders such as onNodeWithText and onNodeWithTag.
sources.title: Testing your Compose layout

questions.explanation: Compose test finders use the merged tree by default, so a Button and its text children form one node that holds all the text values. Matching on '$20' finds the button, but its text is not exactly '$20'. `useUnmergedTree = true` reaches the child `Text` nodes.

questions.prompt: An off-screen item in a `LazyColumn` has been composed but scrolled out of view. Which assertion is true for it?

choices.text: `assertIsDisplayed()` passes for this off-screen node simply because Compose has already composed it once during the initial layout pass and cached the result
`assertExists()` can pass since the node is in the semantics tree, while `assertIsDisplayed()` fails since it isn't visible in bounds
Both `assertExists()` and `assertIsDisplayed()` fail on it, because Compose eagerly removes every off-screen node from the tree
`assertDoesNotExist()` passes on this node, because that assertion actually checks on-screen visibility rather than tree presence

sources.claim: assertExists only confirms the node exists in the semantics tree; assertIsDisplayed confirms it exists and is visible within bounds; performScrollToNode scrolls to a node.
sources.title: Testing APIs (Compose)

questions.explanation: `assertExists()` only checks that the node is in the semantics tree; `assertIsDisplayed()` also requires it to be visible on screen within bounds. `assertDoesNotExist()` checks presence in the tree, not visibility. To check an item that is not composed yet, scroll with `performScrollToNode` first.

questions.prompt: You want to assert the midpoint of a 300 ms Compose animation. By default the assertion always sees the end state. What do you do?

choices.text: Add a plain `Thread.sleep(150)` call on the test thread right before running the assertion against the animated composable
Wrap the assertion in `runBlocking { delay(150) }` so real wall-clock time passes before the check against the animated node runs
Register a custom `IdlingResource` that simply reports itself as busy for a fixed 150 ms window around the animation
Set `composeTestRule.mainClock.autoAdvance = false`, trigger it, then `mainClock.advanceTimeBy(150)` before asserting

sources.claim: Compose tests are synchronized by default and use a virtual clock; set composeTestRule.mainClock.autoAdvance = false and advance with advanceTimeByFrame or advanceTimeBy; register idling resources for background work unknown to Compose.
sources.title: Synchronize your tests (Compose)

questions.explanation: Compose tests are synchronized with the UI and use a virtual clock that advances until idle before assertions, so animations finish first. Turning off `autoAdvance` and advancing the clock by hand lets you observe intermediate frames. Real-time sleeps and delays don't drive the virtual clock and make tests flaky, and idling resources are for background work Compose doesn't know about.

questions.prompt: Which test is the poorest fit for Robolectric according to Android's guidance?

choices.text: A Compose test that clicks a button and checks that an on-screen counter's displayed text is updated to the expected new value
A test that checks a screen's state handling and recomposition after a sequence of simulated text-field input changes
A test of edge-to-edge insets and picture-in-picture behaviour, or a screen that relies on `WebView`
A quick screenshot test of an isolated component, taken where pixel-perfect rendering accuracy isn't considered critical

sources.claim: Robolectric doesn't support all features and APIs; use it for isolated UI behavior and screenshots where pixel accuracy isn't critical; use device tests for system UI features like edge-to-edge and picture-in-picture and unsupported features like WebView.
sources.title: Robolectric strategies

questions.explanation: Robolectric simulates Android on the JVM and is fast, but it has no real screen and only partial support for some APIs. The guide recommends device tests for system UI features such as edge-to-edge and picture-in-picture and for unsupported features like `WebView`. Isolated UI behaviour and approximate screenshots are good Robolectric uses.

questions.prompt: Your team records screenshot reference images on their Macs, and the Linux CI job keeps failing with tiny text and shadow differences. What is the recommended remedy?

choices.text: Generate and update reference images in one consistent environment such as CI, and configure a tolerance for small pixel differences
Delete the screenshot tests entirely, since rendering differs so much between operating systems that they can never be made to work reliably across a team
Record all reference images at a much lower resolution than the real device, so subtle text and shadow differences disappear
Run screenshot tests only on developers' own Mac machines and skip running or validating them at all inside Linux CI jobs

sources.claim: If you develop on a Mac and save new screenshots locally, you might see broken tests on a Linux CI machine; tolerate small changes with thresholds or take screenshots on a server.
sources.title: Screenshot testing

questions.explanation: Screenshot tests depend on low-level platform drawing (text, shadows) that differs between operating systems and hardware, so references from a Mac can fail on Linux CI. The guidance is to tolerate small differences with a threshold or smart differ, and to take the screenshots on a server in consistent conditions.

questions.prompt: A Compose UI test for a list screen passes locally but fails intermittently in CI: the list loads from a repository on a background dispatcher, and the test asserts the first item right after launch. Explain why this happens and how to fix it properly.

sources.claim: Compose tests synchronize with the UI and a virtual clock; use waitUntil or waitUntilAtLeastOneExists for conditions, and register idling resources for background work unknown to Compose.
sources.title: Synchronize your tests (Compose)

sources.claim: Avoid sleeps, which make tests slow or flaky; use idling resources in small UI tests and wait-until APIs in bigger ones; replace modules with test versions such as TestDispatcher.
sources.title: Big test stability

questions.explanation: Senior answers explain what Compose's automatic synchronization covers and what it doesn't, then choose determinism (fakes) first and conditional waits second.

model_answer.summary: Compose synchronizes with its own recomposition and virtual clock, but not with background work it can't see, so the assertion can run before data arrives. Fix it by injecting a fake repository or a test dispatcher so loading is deterministic, or by waiting on a condition with `waitUntil`-style APIs or an idling resource, never with sleeps.
key_points: Compose test rules wait for the UI to be idle, but background loading on other dispatchers is invisible to them
Best fix: test the screen in isolation with fake state or a fake repository, so no real async work happens
Otherwise wait on a condition: `waitUntilAtLeastOneExists(hasText(...))` or `waitUntil { ... }` with a timeout
Or register an `IdlingResource` that tracks the background work, or use a `TestDispatcher`
Never use `Thread.sleep`, which is slow and still flaky across environments

questions.prompt: Your team wants to move most Compose UI tests from emulators to Robolectric to speed up CI. Give your recommendation, including what you would keep on devices and why.

sources.claim: Robolectric runs tests in a simulated Android environment inside a JVM without emulator overhead and flakiness; it doesn't support all APIs; any UI test in the test source set runs with Robolectric.
sources.title: Robolectric strategies

sources.claim: Big local tests can use simulators like Robolectric to test larger portions of the app on the host.
sources.title: Fundamentals of testing Android apps

questions.explanation: The balanced senior answer uses Robolectric to widen the fast layer of the pyramid without pretending it replaces device coverage.

model_answer.summary: Move isolated component and screen behaviour tests to Robolectric (the `test` source set) for speed and stability, but keep a smaller set of device tests for system integration, real rendering and APIs Robolectric doesn't fully support. Think in terms of fidelity versus speed.
key_points: Robolectric runs a simulated Android on the JVM: fast and without emulator flakiness, and UI tests in the `test` source set run on it
It is not a full emulator: no real screen and partial API support, so fidelity is lower
Good fits: state and click behaviour of screens and components, and screenshots where pixel accuracy isn't critical
Keep on devices: edge-to-edge and insets, picture-in-picture, `WebView`, and critical end-to-end journeys
Enable `isIncludeAndroidResources` and keep composables testable in isolation

questions.prompt: You are adding screenshot tests to protect your design system components. Describe how you would set them up, how you choose what to screenshot, and how you keep them from becoming noisy.

sources.claim: Previews marked @PreviewTest in the screenshotTest source set; updateScreenshotTest generates reference images and validateScreenshotTest compares, producing an HTML report on mismatch; tests run host-side.
sources.title: Compose Preview Screenshot Testing

sources.claim: Minimize the number of screenshot tests while maximizing feedback; avoid combinations of all scenarios; platform differences mean tolerating small changes or generating screenshots on a server.
sources.title: Screenshot testing

questions.explanation: Senior answers treat screenshot tests as a cost-benefit decision: high coverage per test, but maintenance and noise grow with the number of combinations, so they curate.

model_answer.summary: Use host-side screenshot tests (such as Compose Preview Screenshot Testing with `@PreviewTest` previews in the `screenshotTest` source set) for components. Generate references in CI, choose previews that each give unique feedback rather than every combination, and use tolerances and the diff report to triage.
key_points: Screenshot tests compare against reference images and check colours, margins, sizes and fonts in one test, which suits design system components

Compose Preview Screenshot Testing: `@PreviewTest` previews in `src/screenshotTest`, `updateDebugScreenshotTest` records references and `validateDebugScreenshotTest` compares them, producing an HTML diff report
Pick previews that give unique feedback (for example light/dark, or one large font scale) instead of every combination
Generate references in one consistent environment (CI) and allow small tolerances, since rendering differs across operating systems
Review reference updates in PRs like code, so intentional visual changes are approved

questions.prompt: You want CI to run instrumented tests on a consistent emulator without scripting emulator start-up. With Gradle Managed Devices, what does that look like?

choices.text: Devices are declared in `testOptions.managedDevices` and run with a task like `pixel2api30DebugAndroidTest`; AGP owns the lifecycle
You must still start an emulator by hand from Android Studio or the command line, then run `connectedAndroidTest` against it
Gradle Managed Devices only work with physical hardware devices connected to the CI machine over a USB cable
Gradle Managed Devices actually run the instrumented tests on the JVM through Robolectric rather than a real or virtual device

sources.claim: Build-managed devices are configured in Gradle, and AGP manages their lifecycle; tasks follow <device><variant>AndroidTest; ATD images remove pre-installed apps and disable hardware rendering; use -Pandroid.testoptions.manageddevices.emulator.gpu=swiftshader_indirect on headless CI.
sources.title: Scale your tests with build-managed devices

questions.explanation: Build-managed devices are declared in Gradle; AGP handles create, run and teardown, uses snapshots for fast, clean devices, and exposes tasks named `<device><variant>AndroidTest`. Automated Test Device images remove preinstalled apps and disable hardware rendering for CI, and headless CI can use `swiftshader_indirect`. They are real emulators, not Robolectric.

questions.prompt: An Espresso test sometimes fails because it checks a result that loads from a database in the background. A teammate adds `Thread.sleep(2000)`. Why is this the wrong fix, and what should be used instead?

choices.text: It is fine as written, since two full seconds is long enough to cover the database read time on essentially every real device
Sleeps are slow and still flaky since timing varies by environment; use Idling Resources, or wait-until conditions in bigger tests
Sleeps are only wrong because `Thread.sleep` blocks the main thread; replacing it with a coroutine `delay(2000)` call fixes it
The correct fix is to configure the test runner to retry this test up to three times and simply accept the remaining flakiness

sources.claim: Avoid pausing tests for an arbitrary period (sleep), which makes tests slow or flaky; use Idling Resources in small UI tests and wait-until APIs in bigger tests; replace modules with test versions such as TestDispatcher.
sources.title: Big test stability

questions.explanation: Background work the test framework doesn't know about causes races. Fixed sleeps make tests slower and still fail when an environment needs more time. The guidance is Idling Resources for small UI tests and wait-until APIs for bigger ones, plus test replacements such as `TestDispatcher`. Retries help with infrastructure noise but don't fix the race.

questions.prompt: Instrumented tests pass alone but fail when the full suite runs, because earlier tests leave data in shared preferences and one crashing test aborts the run. Which tool addresses both problems?

choices.text: Android Test Orchestrator with `clearPackageData`: each test gets its own `Instrumentation`, isolating crashes and clearing app data
Adding `@FlakyTest` annotations to the affected tests, which tells the runner to silently skip them whenever they fail
Running the whole instrumented suite on Robolectric instead, since its simulated environment never leaks state between test classes
Increasing the emulator's allocated RAM and CPU cores in the CI configuration so the whole suite finishes running faster

sources.claim: Android Test Orchestrator runs each test in its own Instrumentation invocation, isolating crashes; clearPackageData removes all shared state; execution time may increase; enable with execution = ANDROIDX_TEST_ORCHESTRATOR.
sources.title: AndroidJUnitRunner

questions.explanation: The Orchestrator runs each test in its own `Instrumentation`, so a crash takes down only that test, and `clearPackageData` runs `pm clear` after each one to remove shared state. The trade-off is longer runs because the app restarts per test. The other options don't address shared state or crash isolation.

questions.prompt: Management wants a hard 95% line-coverage gate on the whole Android codebase. What is the strongest argument against it?

choices.text: Coverage instrumentation tools are fundamentally unable to measure Kotlin code correctly and only report accurate numbers for Java
A high number doesn't show the tests are good; a hard target encourages gaming, such as tests with no real assertions
Any coverage target set above roughly 50% always slows the build so much that it becomes impractical for a large codebase
A 95% gate is set far too low to be meaningful; only a strict, unconditional 100% line-coverage target is worth enforcing

sources.claim: Test coverage is a useful tool for finding untested parts of a codebase, but of little use as a numeric statement of how good your tests are; mandated targets lead to gaming such as tests without assertions.
sources.title: TestCoverage

sources.claim: High coverage doesn't guarantee quality; suggested guidelines are 60% acceptable, 75% commendable, 90% exemplary; prioritize coverage of changed code and avoid targets that encourage gaming.
sources.title: Code Coverage Best Practices

questions.explanation: Coverage is useful for finding untested code but says little about test quality: lines can run without their behaviour being checked. Mandated numbers invite gaming. Google's guidance treats about 60% as acceptable, 75% as commendable and 90% as exemplary, and recommends focusing on coverage of changed code rather than a single global gate.

questions.prompt: A function has 100% line coverage, yet a bug in one branch of `isSquare(s) || (isBlue(s) && !isCircle(s))` reaches production. What does this show?

choices.text: The coverage tool must have been misconfigured, since a genuine 100% line-coverage result always means every logical path was tested
The bug must actually live in a third-party library dependency, since a line of application code that ran under test can't itself contain a bug
Branch coverage on this same function would necessarily also report 100%, since it is derived directly from the line-coverage figure
Line coverage counts executed lines, not conditions, so a line can be covered while some logical branches are never checked

sources.claim: A boolean expression such as isSquare(shape) || (isBlue(shape) && !isCircle(shape)) can show full line coverage while only one condition's path was tested; mutation testing helps find such gaps.
sources.title: Code Coverage Best Practices

questions.explanation: Running a line once counts it as covered even if only one side of a compound condition was ever evaluated. That is why coverage is a signal of untested code, not proof of good tests. Branch or condition coverage and mutation testing find more of these gaps.

questions.prompt: Design the test stages of a GitHub Actions pipeline for an Android app so every pull request gets fast feedback, but all test types still run. Say what runs when and how you keep instrumented tests reliable.

sources.claim: Unit and component tests run on every commit, feature tests pre-merge, application tests post-merge, and release candidate tests on minified builds pre-release.
sources.title: Testing strategies

sources.claim: Gradle Managed Devices use snapshots to restore a clean state, support sharding via numManagedDeviceShards, and offer ATD images optimized for CI.
sources.title: Scale your tests with build-managed devices

questions.explanation: Senior pipelines follow the test pyramid in time as well as count: the cheapest, most frequent checks run first. They separate infrastructure flakiness (retry) from test flakiness (fix).

model_answer.summary: Run cheap checks first and fail fast: lint and local unit tests (including Robolectric and screenshot validation), then instrumented tests on Gradle Managed Devices (ATD images, sharded) before merge, with bigger app-level and release-candidate suites after merge or before release. Upload reports as artifacts.
key_points: Stage 1 (every PR, fail fast): build, lint and `./gradlew test` for unit, ViewModel, Robolectric and screenshot validation
Stage 2 (pre-merge): instrumented tests on Gradle Managed Devices with ATD images and `swiftshader_indirect` on headless runners, sharded for speed
Post-merge or pre-release: application-level and minified release-candidate tests across multiple devices
Reliability: device snapshots give clean state, retries only for infrastructure failures, and Orchestrator where shared state matters
Publish test reports and screenshot diffs as artifacts so failures are actionable

questions.prompt: Your CI has a 7% flaky failure rate on UI tests and developers have started re-running jobs without looking. How do you tackle this as the senior engineer?

sources.claim: Flakiness comes from asynchronous operations unknown to the test and from sleeps; fix with idling resources, wait-until APIs and test replacements such as TestDispatcher; add retries at the JUnit, CI or device level, such as Gradle Managed Devices.
sources.title: Big test stability

sources.claim: Orchestrator runs each test in its own Instrumentation; clearPackageData removes shared state between tests.
sources.title: AndroidJUnitRunner

questions.explanation: What separates a senior answer is treating flakiness as a trust and culture problem as well as a technical one: restore the signal (quarantine, metrics) while fixing the root causes.

model_answer.summary: Measure and quarantine first: track flaky tests, then fix root causes, most often synchronization (sleeps, untracked background work, animations), shared state between tests, and real network or backend dependencies. Use hermetic fakes, idling or wait-until APIs, Orchestrator isolation, and managed devices with infrastructure-level retries.
key_points: Track flakiness per test (re-run history) and quarantine the worst offenders so the signal is trusted again, with owners and deadlines
Fix synchronization: remove sleeps, use Idling Resources or `waitUntil` APIs, and `TestDispatcher`s for coroutines
Remove shared state with Orchestrator and `clearPackageData`, and keep tests independent of order
Make tests hermetic: fake the network and backend instead of calling real services
Keep retries for infrastructure (emulator disconnects), for example with Gradle Managed Devices, not to hide test bugs

questions.prompt: A reviewer of your take-home says: 'Coverage is 92%, yet the offline case is broken.' Walk through how you would respond and how you would present your testing in a take-home.

sources.claim: Coverage is useful for finding untested parts of a codebase but of little use as a numeric statement of how good your tests are.
sources.title: TestCoverage

sources.claim: Repository tests should cover online/offline and with/without cached data; add a README that pastes the rubric and marks each item done, and discusses incomplete items.
sources.title: Android job interview take-home test cheat sheet

questions.explanation: Reviewers reward candidates who talk about behaviours and risk rather than percentages. Knowing why coverage misleads, and fixing the gap without getting defensive, is the senior signal.

model_answer.summary: Accept that coverage measured which lines ran, not whether the risky behaviours were checked. Present testing by behaviour: which scenarios from the rubric are tested (offline, cached, error, retry), at which layer, with which doubles, and what is left out. Use coverage only to find untested areas.
key_points: High coverage doesn't show that edge cases such as offline-with-cache were checked; lines can run without meaningful assertions
Use coverage to find untested code, not as proof of quality; focus on the changed and risky code
Organize tests by rubric scenarios: online, offline with and without cache, errors, retry, and config changes
Add the missing repository test for the offline path using fakes, then explain it in the README
In the README, map rubric items to tests and state trade-offs and next steps

questions.prompt: Which statements match Android guidance on test doubles? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A fake provides a working implementation suited to tests.
A mock can verify that a method was called exactly once.
A stub fails a test when its call order differs from expectations.
A fake requires a mocking framework to implement its behavior.
A spy replaces the wrapped object with an in-memory database.

questions.explanation: a is correct: A fake implements behavior for tests. b is correct: Mocks enforce specified interactions, including call counts. c is incorrect: A stub has no interaction expectations. d is incorrect: Fakes need no mocking framework. e is incorrect: A spy wraps a real object and records information.

sources.claim: Fakes have working test implementations without a mocking framework; mocks enforce interactions; stubs have no interaction expectations and spies wrap real objects.
sources.title: Use test doubles in Android

questions.prompt: Which changes make a Fragment with data access logic easier to test? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Keep repository construction inside the Fragment for tighter coupling.
Move business logic out of the Fragment into separate layers.
Replace injected interfaces with concrete network clients in tests.
Make dependencies replaceable through interfaces and injection.
Inject dispatchers so tests can substitute a TestDispatcher.

questions.explanation: a is incorrect: Tight coupling makes isolated testing harder. b is correct: Framework entry points should delegate UI and business logic. c is incorrect: Concrete clients make dependencies harder to replace. d is correct: Replaceable dependencies support isolated tests. e is correct: Injected test dispatchers give predictable scheduling.

sources.claim: Move logic out of activities and fragments, split into layers, avoid framework dependencies in business logic and make dependencies replaceable with interfaces and injection.
sources.title: Fundamentals of testing Android apps

sources.claim: Inject TestDispatchers sharing one scheduler; StandardTestDispatcher queues work and UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts eagerly; replace Main in local tests and use backgroundScope for long-running collectors.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin coroutines on Android

questions.prompt: With limited time for an Android feature, which choices follow the testing pyramid? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Write many small tests that provide fast, reliable feedback.
Use a smaller set of broad tests for higher-fidelity checks.
Make every test end-to-end because broader scope is always cheaper.
Assume small tests need more complex setup than broad tests.
Balance test scope against the cost of finding bugs early.

questions.explanation: a is correct: Small tests form the broad base of the pyramid. b is correct: Big tests offer higher fidelity and form a smaller tip. c is incorrect: Big tests require more setup and maintenance. d is incorrect: Small tests isolate a small portion of code and are simpler. e is correct: The strategy seeks early feedback and lower bug costs.

sources.claim: Use many small tests and relatively few big tests; unit and component tests run on each commit and release-candidate tests use minified builds before release.
sources.title: Testing strategies

questions.prompt: Which statements describe local coroutine tests using TestDispatchers? Select all that apply.

choices.text: StandardTestDispatcher queues new coroutines until the test yields.
Each TestDispatcher should use a separate virtual-time scheduler.
Replace unavailable Main with setMain and reset it after the test.
UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts new coroutines eagerly.
Thread.sleep advances the shared scheduler to run queued work.

questions.explanation: a is correct: StandardTestDispatcher provides explicit scheduling control. b is incorrect: All test dispatchers should share a scheduler. c is correct: Local tests lack the Android Main dispatcher. d is correct: UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts eagerly, though suspension can pause work. e is incorrect: Scheduler APIs or yielding run queued tasks; sleeping does not.

sources.claim: Inject TestDispatchers sharing one scheduler; StandardTestDispatcher queues work and UnconfinedTestDispatcher starts eagerly; replace Main in local tests and use backgroundScope for long-running collectors.
sources.title: Testing Kotlin coroutines on Android

questions.prompt: Which statements describe Turbine Flow assertions? Select all that apply.

choices.text: awaitItem checks the next emitted item.
Unconsumed events are silently ignored when the test block ends.
awaitError consumes and checks a Flow termination error.
awaitComplete is used to consume an ordinary emitted list.
cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents deliberately discards remaining events.

questions.explanation: a is correct: awaitItem receives the next item for assertions. b is incorrect: Unconsumed events fail the test. c is correct: Flow errors are events that awaitError consumes. d is incorrect: awaitComplete expects completion, not an item. e is correct: The API explicitly permits ignoring remaining events.

sources.claim: awaitItem, awaitError and awaitComplete consume distinct events; unconsumed events fail the test unless explicitly ignored with cancelAndIgnoreRemainingEvents.
sources.title: Turbine

questions.prompt: Which setup follows Room database testing guidance? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Create an in-memory database for hermetic query tests.
Replace DAO queries with mocks to verify their SQL semantics.
Close the database after each test.
Run the documented database tests on an Android device.
Reuse a production on-disk database to preserve isolation between tests.

questions.explanation: a is correct: An in-memory database isolates test data. b is incorrect: A mocked query does not execute the SQL being tested. c is correct: The example closes the database in After. d is correct: The guide recommends testing the database on a device. e is incorrect: Shared persistent production data defeats hermetic testing.

sources.claim: Use an in-memory Room database for hermetic query tests on a device and close it after each test.
sources.title: Test and debug your database

questions.prompt: A Compose test asserts before background data loading finishes. Which remedies follow the testing guidance? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Assume Compose automatically tracks every background dispatcher.
Wait for a UI condition with a waitUntil API.
Add a fixed sleep that is long enough on the local workstation.
Register an idling resource for otherwise untracked work.
Replace asynchronous modules with controllable test versions.

questions.explanation: a is incorrect: Background operations unknown to the test are not automatically tracked. b is correct: Condition-based waiting synchronizes with actual progress. c is incorrect: Fixed sleeps can be slow or flaky in different environments. d is correct: Idling resources track work outside Compose. e is correct: Test replacements such as TestDispatcher improve synchronization.

sources.claim: Compose synchronization does not track arbitrary external work; use waitUntil conditions or registered idling resources to track it.
sources.title: Synchronize your tests (Compose)

sources.claim: Untracked asynchronous work causes flakiness; use idling resources and test replacements rather than arbitrary sleeps.

questions.prompt: Which statements support deciding where to run Robolectric UI tests? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Robolectric simulates Android locally without emulator overhead.
Robolectric supports every Android API with production fidelity.
UI tests can run in the test source set with Robolectric configured.
Moving tests to Robolectric guarantees device-specific issues disappear.
Robolectric can run Compose and Espresso UI tests.

questions.explanation: a is correct: The local JVM simulator avoids emulator overhead. b is incorrect: The guide notes incomplete API support. c is correct: The documented setup uses the test source set. d is incorrect: Incomplete simulation cannot guarantee device behavior. e is correct: Both UI testing frameworks are supported.

sources.claim: Robolectric simulates Android locally, supports Compose and Espresso tests in the test source set, and does not support every Android API.
sources.title: Robolectric strategies

questions.prompt: Which practices keep screenshot tests useful? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Compare the new screenshot with a previously approved reference.
Generate every possible configuration combination regardless of feedback.
Select a small set of scenarios that maximize useful feedback.
Review differences before approving a replacement reference image.
Require exact equality across operating systems without considering rendering differences.

questions.explanation: a is correct: Reference images define approved appearance. b is incorrect: The guide recommends minimizing count while maximizing feedback. c is correct: Representative scenarios reduce unnecessary combinations. d is correct: A diff can expose a bug or an intentional change requiring approval. e is incorrect: Platform differences can require tolerances or a consistent rendering environment.

sources.claim: Compare screenshots with approved references, review differences, minimize tests while maximizing feedback, and account for rendering differences across platforms.
sources.title: Screenshot testing

questions.prompt: Which decisions follow Android guidance for test stages and managed devices? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Run small unit and component tests on every commit.
Postpone all unit tests until a minified release build is ready.
Use managed-device snapshots to restore a clean test state.
Run release-candidate tests on minified builds before release.
Treat managed-device sharding as a substitute for executing assertions.

questions.explanation: a is correct: Small tests provide feedback on each commit. b is incorrect: Waiting until release delays detection of basic bugs. c is correct: Managed devices restore snapshots for a clean state. d is correct: Release candidates need checks against minified builds. e is incorrect: Sharding divides tests across devices; assertions still execute.

sources.claim: Use many small tests and relatively few big tests; unit and component tests run on each commit and release-candidate tests use minified builds before release.

sources.claim: Managed devices restore snapshots to clean state and support dividing test execution across shards.

questions.prompt: Which changes address flaky UI tests and shared app state? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Add an arbitrary fixed sleep before every assertion so any background operation is guaranteed to finish in all environments.
Track background operations with idling resources or test replacements.
Rely on a fixed test order to retain data from earlier tests.
Use Orchestrator to run tests in separate Instrumentation instances.
Use clearPackageData with Orchestrator to remove shared app state.

sources.claim: Untracked asynchronous work causes flakiness; use idling resources and test replacements rather than arbitrary sleeps.

questions.prompt: A test suite reports high code coverage but misses an offline bug. Which statements about coverage are valid? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Coverage helps locate code that has not been exercised.
A high percentage establishes that assertions verify the important behavior.
Low coverage indicates parts of the codebase need investigation.
Reaching full line coverage guarantees every input case is correct.
Use coverage to investigate gaps rather than as a numeric quality verdict.

questions.explanation: a is correct: Finding untested areas is a useful purpose of coverage. b is incorrect: Executing code does not establish test quality. c is correct: Unexercised code is a useful starting point for investigation. d is incorrect: Line execution does not prove all behaviors or inputs. e is correct: The author warns against treating the number as test quality.

sources.claim: Coverage helps find untested parts of a codebase but is of little use as a numeric statement of test quality.
